screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore Dynamic Multipoint VPN, a design pattern that removes the N-squared tunnel problem by combining multipoint GRE, NHRP, and IPsec. You will learn why DMVPN is used in large enterprise deployments, how the hub and spokes cooperate, and which parts handle address resolution, routing, and security. We will use a concrete three-router scenario — a hub and two spokes — to make the concepts tangible. First, you will understand how mGRE provides a single logical tunnel interface that can terminate many spokes, avoiding dozens or hundreds of unique point-to-point tunnels. Finally, we'll preview Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 trade-offs so you can choose the right model for performance and scalability. As you go through the lesson screens, watch how configuration fragments map to each concept and how simple verification commands reveal the system state. By the end you'll know not just the commands, but how to reason about routing, secure tunnels, and common troubleshooting checks. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Dynamic Multipoint VPN
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Dynamic Multipoint VPN

A practical pattern for connecting many branch sites to a hub with secure, on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels.

In this lesson
How mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec work together to deliver scalable VPNs and how phases change routing behavior.
Practical demo
Step-by-step hub and spoke configuration using IKEv2/IPsec and EIGRP over the DMVPN tunnel network.
What you'll practice
NHRP registration checks, verifying IPsec SAs, and validating dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels with pings.
Explore Key Topics
mGRE
Single logical tunnel that terminates multiple spokes; avoids many point-to-point tunnels.
NHRP
Maps tunnel IPs to public IPs so spokes can form direct shortcuts on demand.
IPsec
Use a reusable IPsec profile with IKEv2 and an ESP transform to secure GRE traffic across the internet.
Architecture snapshot
Hub (NHRP Server)
Single mGRE interface, NHRP mappings, IPsec profile applied.
Spokes (NHRP Clients)
Register tunnel IPs and learn other spokes' public IPs via the hub.
Routing
EIGRP or OSPF run over the tunnel; multicast mapping is important for OSPF on NBMA clouds.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will describe the architecture and key components of DMVPN, identify how mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec interact, and differentiate the three DMVPN phases and their trade-offs. You will be able to configure a Phase 2 hub-and-spoke DMVPN using IKEv2 and an IPsec profile on Cisco IOS-XE, then integrate a dynamic routing protocol like EIGRP or OSPF to carry internal routes across the DMVPN cloud. Finally, you will learn a troubleshooting workflow: verify public reachability, check NHRP registrations, inspect IPsec SAs, and validate routing adjacencies. Each objective focuses on practical competence: you will read configuration fragments, run verification commands, and interpret outputs to make repair decisions quickly. These skills matter because real-world DMVPNs support many branches and must scale securely; misconfigurations in NHRP, IPsec, or routing type can cause traffic black-holing or slow spoke-to-spoke startup. Expect hands-on practice with the three-router scenario to anchor these objectives in a concrete network.

Hands-on Lab Checklist

Verification commands

Common checklist errors

screens.title: What problem does DMVPN solve?
screens.narratorSegment: DMVPN solves a fundamental scalability problem in traditional site-to-site VPN designs: the N-squared tunnel explosion. In a full-mesh design each site needs a separate point-to-point tunnel to every other site, which becomes unmanageable as the number of branches grows. DMVPN replaces that static mesh with a single logical multipoint cloud and the ability for spokes to form direct shortcuts when needed. Concretely, this means you configure one mGRE interface on the hub and matching mGRE interfaces on spokes instead of creating many tunnel interfaces. When a spoke wants to reach another spoke it asks the hub for the other spoke's public IP using NHRP and then builds a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel. That dynamic behavior reduces configuration errors and conserves hub bandwidth when spokes talk directly to each other. A common misconception is that DMVPN removes the need for a hub — it does not; the hub is still the registration authority and often the path for multicast or initial control plane traffic. What DMVPN removes is the need for pre-provisioned point-to-point tunnels between every pair of spokes. Think of DMVPN as a taxi-hail system where the hub knows every vehicle's location and directs riders to a direct ride when possible rather than routing each trip through a single central depot. How might this change your network operations when you add dozens of branches?

keyIdea.text: DMVPN reduces operational and configuration complexity by enabling on-demand spoke-to-spoke tunnels instead of static full-mesh tunnels.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why use DMVPN?

DMVPN avoids the N-squared tunnel problem by letting spokes dynamically form direct tunnels using address resolution from the hub.

Key details
  • Single mGRE interface on hub terminates many spokes.
  • NHRP maps internal tunnel IPs to public IPs for shortcut creation.
  • IPsec profile secures GRE traffic across the internet.
Key Takeaway

DMVPN trades static tunnels for a dynamic, centrally registered cloud so spokes can build direct tunnels when traffic flows demand it.

Analogy: hub as directory service

Imagine the hub as a directory server that records each spoke's internal address and public reachability. Spokes query the directory only when they need to contact another spoke, then connect directly for efficiency.

Common misconception

Some expect DMVPN to remove the hub entirely. The hub remains essential as the NHRP server and often as the anchor for multicast or initial route distribution.

screens.title: Multipoint GRE (mGRE)
screens.narratorSegment: Multipoint GRE is the foundation that allows DMVPN to scale. Unlike point-to-point GRE, which binds one tunnel interface to a single remote IP, mGRE lets a single tunnel interface accept traffic from many peers without preconfigured destinations. On the hub you configure tunnel mode gre multipoint and a tunnel IP. Spokes configure mGRE as well but initially have their tunnel destination set to the hub's public address for registration. Because the mGRE interface behaves like a non-broadcast multi-access network, devices cannot discover neighbors by simple broadcast and require a discovery mechanism for mapping logical addresses to physical endpoints. This is where NHRP enters. A practical implication is that the hub's tunnel interface must be designed to handle all incoming GRE encapsulated packets and the IPsec profile attached to that interface must be able to secure traffic from any spoke endpoint. A pitfall operators often see is forgetting to set ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to accommodate GRE plus IPsec overhead; this can cause fragmentation or application-level issues. Example: in the lab the hub uses Tunnel0 with 172.16.0.1 and ip mtu 1400 so GRE-over-IPsec packets avoid fragmentation. Remember: mGRE simplifies configuration, but you must plan MTU and security for the multi-tenant tunnel endpoint.

keyIdea.title: mGRE role
keyIdea.text: mGRE provides a single logical tunnel interface that can carry traffic for multiple tunnel peers, enabling one hub to serve many spokes.

content.html:
Definition

Multipoint GRE interface

A logical tunnel interface configured to accept GRE traffic from many peers instead of a single destination.

Practical settings
  • tunnel mode gre multipoint
  • ip mtu 1400 and ip tcp adjust-mss 1360 to avoid fragmentation
  • apply a crypto ipsec profile to the tunnel interface
Operator tip

Ensure the hub's physical interface and CPU can handle aggregated encapsulation and IPsec processing when many spokes are active.

mGRE behavior visualized
Think of the mGRE interface as a virtual LAN where every spoke has a tunnel IP. The hub accepts packets from any spoke and forwards logically based on routing or NHRP resolution.
Common mistake

Forgetting MTU adjustments for GRE over IPsec leads to intermittent application problems. Always set ip mtu and adjust MSS on the tunnel interface.

screens.title: Next-Hop Resolution Protocol (NHRP)
screens.narratorSegment: NHRP is the discovery and mapping service that DMVPN uses to match logical tunnel IPs to public physical IPs. The hub acts as the NHRP server, or Next-Hop Server, and every spoke is a client that registers its tunnel IP and public address. When Spoke A wants to send traffic to Spoke B it first consults the hub by querying NHRP for the target's public IP. The hub replies with the mapping and then Spoke A builds a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel to Spoke B. This process is the dynamic shortcut mechanism that keeps traffic off the hub when possible. A concrete example from our lab: R2 registers 172.16.0.2 with the hub; when R2 needs 172.16.0.3 it asks the hub which returns 203.0.113.3, enabling a direct tunnel. A common misinterpretation is to assume NHRP itself carries routing information; it does not. NHRP only resolves addresses. Routing is handled by your dynamic routing protocol over the tunnels. Another operational note: ensure ip nhrp network-id values match across devices; mismatched network-ids prevent registrations. Finish by asking yourself how you would verify NHRP mappings quickly if a spoke reports it cannot reach another spoke.

keyIdea.title: NHRP role
keyIdea.text: NHRP maps internal tunnel addresses to public endpoints and enables dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnel formation when needed.

content.html:
Process Flow

NHRP registration and resolution

1. Spoke registers
Spoke sends its tunnel IP and public IP to the hub (NHS) with ip nhrp nhs configured.
2. Query for destination
When a spoke needs another spoke, it queries the NHS for the other spoke's public IP.
3. Direct tunnel formed
Spoke builds a GRE-over-IPsec tunnel to the returned public IP and traffic flows directly.
Example

R2 registers 172.16.0.2 → 203.0.113.2 with R1. When R2 pings 172.16.0.3, R1 replies with 203.0.113.3 so R2 can build a direct tunnel to R3.

Verification
  • show ip nhrp on hub — lists registered spokes
  • show ip nhrp on spoke — shows NHS and mappings
Misconception check

NHRP does not advertise routing prefixes; it only maps tunnel addresses to public addresses. Routing remains the job of EIGRP or OSPF.

screens.title: IPsec + IKEv2 integration
screens.narratorSegment: IPsec provides confidentiality and integrity for GRE-encapsulated DMVPN traffic. The modern best practice is to bind an IPsec profile to the mGRE tunnel interface instead of applying transform sets per peer. An IPsec profile references an IKEv2 profile for key exchange and a transform set for the data plane. Using an IPsec profile simplifies management because the profile applies to any peer that establishes a GRE session over the tunnel, avoiding per-peer crypto map complexity. In our lab we assume a COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE and COHORTIA_IKEV2_PROFILE are already defined; the tunnel interface simply references the profile with the crypto ipsec profile command. A common pitfall is forgetting NAT traversal: if a spoke or hub is behind NAT, you must allow UDP 4500 and 500 and ensure the IKEv2 profile negotiates NAT-T. Another operational note is to inspect IPsec SAs with show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa to confirm both control and data-plane associations. Example: after a spoke-to-spoke shortcut forms, you will see an ephemeral IPsec SA on each spoke corresponding to the direct GRE peer. Verify both sides to confirm symmetric SAs. Remember that security configuration and address resolution are separate responsibilities: NHRP resolves addresses, IPsec secures the resulting GRE tunnels.

keyIdea.title: IPsec practice
keyIdea.text: Apply a crypto ipsec profile to the mGRE interface and use IKEv2 for scalable, peer-agnostic key exchange for dynamic tunnels.

content.html:
Definition

IPsec profile fundamentals

Use a crypto ipsec profile referencing an IKEv2 profile so the tunnel interface can accept IPsec SAs from any spoke without per-peer crypto maps.

Operational checklist
  • Define IKEv2 profile and transform-set first.
  • Create an ipsec profile that points to the IKEv2 profile.
  • Apply crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE to Tunnel0.
Verification commands
show crypto ikev2 sa — IKEv2 control plane state
show crypto ipsec sa — ESP data-plane SAs
NAT and ports

Ensure UDP 500 and UDP 4500 are allowed when NAT traversal is required; otherwise peer negotiation may fail.

screens.title: DMVPN Phases at a glance
screens.narratorSegment: DMVPN is commonly discussed in three phases because each phase defines how routing and spoke-to-spoke traffic are handled. Phase 1 is the simplest: hub-and-spoke only. Spoke-to-spoke traffic always traverses the hub, and spokes do not form direct tunnels. This is simple but creates a hub bottleneck. Phase 2 allows spokes to form direct tunnels dynamically using NHRP resolution, but routing may still be hub-centric because the routing protocol advertises spoke networks via the hub. That means the first packet may traverse the hub before the shortcut is built, and care is needed to ensure routing convergence supports shortcuts. Phase 3 moves routing decisions closer to the spokes by allowing NHRP Redirect and Shortcut messages; spokes can learn routes directly and avoid sending initial packets through the hub for route discovery. Phase 3 is the most scalable for many branches, but it requires careful route summarization or modifications at the hub to avoid routing loops. A common misconception is to assume Phase 2 and Phase 3 only change tunnel behavior; they also affect how the routing protocol sees networks. Choose the phase based on whether you prioritize simplicity (Phase 1), quicker path optimization (Phase 2), or fully optimal spoke-to-spoke routing at scale (Phase 3). Which trade-off matters most for your deployment: simplicity or optimal routing?

keyIdea.title: Phase summary
keyIdea.text: Phase 1 forwards everything through the hub, Phase 2 enables dynamic tunnels but keeps hub-centric routing, Phase 3 optimizes routing to allow direct spoke-to-spoke reachability without hub involvement for routing decisions.

content.html:
Phase 1
Hub-and-spoke only
All traffic, including spoke-to-spoke, traverses the hub. No shortcuts are formed. Simple to configure but not optimal for spoke-to-spoke bandwidth.
Phase 2
Dynamic shortcuts
Spokes can build direct tunnels after NHRP resolution. Routing remains hub-centric unless additional steps are taken to advertise routes differently.
Phase 3
Optimal spoke-to-spoke routing
Uses NHRP Redirect and Shortcut so spokes can learn routes directly and avoid hub involvement for routing decisions. Best for large-scale deployments with careful route planning.
Design note

Phase choice affects not just tunnel creation but also how routing protocols converge. Use Phase 3 for scale and performance, but ensure the hub performs appropriate summarization or route manipulation to avoid loops.

screens.title: Phase 1 details — hub-centric behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Phase 1 DMVPN is appropriate when simplicity and strict central control are primary goals. In Phase 1 spokes register with the hub but do not form direct tunnels to other spokes; all traffic is forwarded through the hub. This makes multicast and routing straightforward because the hub remains the single forwarding and registration point. The advantage is ease of configuration and predictable traffic paths. The disadvantage is that spokes communicating with each other use twice the internet bandwidth for the same payload and the hub becomes a potential bottleneck. A concrete example: if Spoke R2 wants to reach Spoke R3 in Phase 1, the packet goes from R2 to the hub's public IP, gets decapsulated and re-encapsulated by the hub, then sent to R3, consuming hub C P U and bandwidth. Operators sometimes mistakenly assume Phase 1 requires less IPsec configuration; in reality, the hub still needs sufficient crypto capacity because it handles all data-plane encryption for spoke traffic. Use Phase 1 in smaller deployments or where policy dictates central inspection or logging of all traffic. Phase 1 details — hub-centric behavior means phase 1 is simplest but forces all spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub, which can cause hub-side bottlenecks.. In practical terms, when all traffic must traverse the hub. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Phase 1 — Hub-and-Spoke

Characteristics

  • No direct spoke-to-spoke tunnels.
  • Hub handles all forwarding and IPsec processing.
  • Simple multicast and routing handling via the hub.
Example flow

R2 → R1 (hub) decapsulate/re-encapsulate → R3. Hub processes both encryption and forwarding steps.

When to choose

Choose Phase 1 for small deployments, strict inspection requirements, or when hub capacity meets expected traffic loads.

screens.title: Phase 2 details — spoke shortcuts
screens.narratorSegment: Phase 2 allows spokes to create direct tunnels to one another after an initial resolution via NHRP. The hub still advertises route information in a hub-centric manner, but once a spoke learns another spoke's public IP it can establish a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel and exchange traffic directly. This reduces the data path length, improving latency and conserving hub bandwidth. In practical terms: a spoke pings a destination, queries the hub, receives the remote public IP, builds a direct tunnel, and then subsequent traffic uses the shortcut. However, routing can still be a source of confusion because routing advertisements may cause traffic to be forwarded via the hub until the shortcut is established. Misconfigurations often relate to OSPF network types or forgetting ip nhrp map multicast dynamic on the hub so multicast routing updates do not flow correctly to spokes. For a lab example, using EIGRP over the tunnel generally works without changing network types, whereas OSPF may require ip ospf network broadcast or non-broadcast settings on the hub to ensure neighbors form correctly over the NBMA cloud. In summary, Phase 2 is a useful middle ground: better than Phase 1 for traffic efficiency, but still requires careful routing behavior checks.

keyIdea.title: Phase 2 benefit
keyIdea.text: Phase 2 supports dynamic spoke-to-spoke shortcuts but often needs routing considerations to avoid initial hub-forwarding surprises.

content.html:
Process

Spoke-to-spoke shortcut lifecycle

  1. Spoke initiates traffic to another spoke.
  2. Spoke queries hub via NHRP for destination's public IP.
  3. Spoke builds direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel and traffic flows directly.
Routing note

EIGRP works well over DMVPN without special network-type commands. OSPF may require explicit network type commands on the hub to properly form neighbors across the NBMA cloud.

Common mistake

Expecting immediate direct traffic: initial packets may still traverse the hub while the NHRP query and shortcut setup complete.

screens.title: Phase 3 details — optimal routing
screens.narratorSegment: Phase 3 introduces NHRP Redirect and Shortcut messages to make routing optimal for spoke-to-spoke communications. Rather than just forming a temporary direct tunnel after address resolution, the hub can send a redirect telling a spoke that a better path exists and provide information so the spokes update routing directly. This lets spokes learn routes from each other in a way that avoids repeated hub involvement for routing decisions. Practically this reduces hub load and avoids hairpinning after the first packet. Implementing Phase 3 requires careful consideration at the hub: you may need to summarize or manipulate advertised routes so the hub's routing entries allow proper redirect behavior without creating loops. A misconception is to assume Phase 3 is a drop-in replacement for Phase 2; routing behavior changes and must be validated in lab conditions. Use Phase 3 when you have many spokes and want the most efficient runtime forwarding, and ensure your routing strategy supports NHRP redirect messaging. As you plan, ask how route advertisement at the hub will affect redirects and whether summarization is necessary to avoid overlapping advertisements.

keyIdea.title: Phase 3 advantage
keyIdea.text: Phase 3 enables the hub to redirect spokes and lets spokes learn routes directly, minimizing hub involvement for routing and improving scale.

content.html:
Process

NHRP Redirect & Shortcut

Hub can inform spokes of better next-hops and enable spokes to learn routes directly, preventing hub hairpinning after the first packet.

Design caution

Ensure the hub's route advertisements are arranged so redirects don't create routing loops; summarization and route selection matter.

When to use

Use Phase 3 for large-scale DMVPNs where spoke-to-spoke communications are frequent and hub load must be minimized.

Misconception check

Phase 3 is not automatically safe for all routing designs; validate route advertisements and summarization plans in the lab to avoid loops.

screens.title: Configuring the Hub (R1) — example
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through a typical hub configuration used in the lab. The hub's Tunnel0 uses a multipoint GRE mode with a tunnel IP of 172.16.0.1. Important operational commands include setting ip mtu to 1400 and ip tcp adjust-mss to 1360 to avoid fragmentation when GRE and IPsec add overhead. The hub must use ip nhrp map multicast dynamic so multicast routing updates reach spokes and the spokes can learn multicast-required protocols. The crypto ipsec profile references the IKEv2 profile so the tunnel automatically negotiates SAs with any spoke. Finally, enable EIGRP on the tunnel network so internal subnets advertise correctly. A common mistake is omitting no ip redirects on the tunnel to avoid forwarding confusion, or leaving mismatched network-id values between hub and spokes. After applying these commands, verify NHRP registrations and EIGRP neighbors with show commands. The configuration below is directly usable in the lab and demonstrates how each command maps to a DMVPN function: addressing, MTU handling, NHRP registration, IPsec security, and routing distribution. Configuring the Hub (R1) — example means configure one mgre tunnel with nhrp server functions, attach an ipsec profile, tune mtu, and run a routing protocol to distribute spoke prefixes.. In practical terms, tunnel, nhrp, ipsec profile, and eigrp setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hub config principle
keyIdea.text: Configure one mGRE tunnel with NHRP server functions, attach an IPsec profile, tune MTU, and run a routing protocol to distribute spoke prefixes.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Hub configuration snippet

interface Tunnel0
 ip address 172.16.0.1 255.255.255.0
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 no ip redirects
 ip nhrp network-id 100
 ip nhrp map multicast dynamic
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/1
 tunnel mode gre multipoint
 crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE

router eigrp 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.0.255
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
 no auto-summary
This snippet ties MTU settings, NHRP server attributes, the mGRE interface, and an IPsec profile together, then advertises the DMVPN tunnel network into EIGRP.
Explanation
  • ip nhrp network-id 100 — shared cloud identifier
  • ip nhrp map multicast dynamic — support multicast routing
  • crypto ipsec profile — secures all spoke connections
Verify
Use show ip nhrp, show crypto ikev2 sa, show crypto ipsec sa, and show ip eigrp neighbors to validate operation.

screens.title: Configuring a Spoke & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: A spoke configuration mirrors the hub in key ways but includes the ip nhrp nhs command so it registers with the hub. The spoke sets a tunnel IP like 172.16.0.2, configures tunnel destination to the hub's public IP so the initial mGRE registration can occur, and references the same IPsec profile. After configuration, verify the registration on the hub with show ip nhrp; the hub should list the spoke's tunnel IP and public IP mapping. If NHRP registration fails, first check ip nhrp network-id consistency and confirm the spoke can reach the hub's public IP using basic IP connectivity. For IPsec issues, inspect show crypto ikev2 sa for the IKE control plane and show crypto ipsec sa for ESP SAs. Routing problems are often caused by incorrect OSPF network-type settings or forgetting to include the tunnel network in the routing process. Also adjust MTU and MSS to handle GRE + IPsec overhead. The lab spoke snippet below uses the recommended values and mapping commands. Finally, to trigger a dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnel, ping a host behind another spoke; then verify the ephemeral IPsec SA appears with show crypto ipsec sa. This verification strategy — connectivity, NHRP, IPsec, and routing — is the most reliable troubleshooting order.

keyIdea.title: Spoke and troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Spokes register with the hub using ip nhrp nhs, apply the IPsec profile, and require the same network-id and MTU settings; verify in this order: IP, NHRP, IPsec, routing.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Spoke configuration snippet

interface Tunnel0
 ip address 172.16.0.2 255.255.255.0
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 no ip redirects
 ip nhrp network-id 100
 ip nhrp nhs 172.16.0.1
 ip nhrp map 172.16.0.1 198.51.100.1
 ip nhrp map multicast 198.51.100.1
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/1
 tunnel destination 198.51.100.1
 tunnel mode gre multipoint
 crypto ipsec profile COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE

router eigrp 1
 network 172.16.0.0 0.0.0.255
 network 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
 no auto-summary
This spoke snippet registers its tunnel address with the hub and maps the hub's tunnel IP to the hub's public IP so initial registration and multicast mapping succeed.
Troubleshooting steps
  1. Confirm public IP connectivity to hub.
  2. Check show ip nhrp for registrations.
  3. Verify show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa.
  4. Validate routing adjacencies (show ip eigrp neighbors).
Common fixes
  • Correct ip nhrp network-id mismatches.
  • Open UDP 500/4500 on firewalls if NAT-T is present.
  • Adjust MTU/MSS to avoid fragmentation for GRE over IPsec.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important facts. First, DMVPN combines mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec to let spokes create on-demand tunnels that scale far better than static full-mesh VPNs. Second, mGRE provides a single logical tunnel endpoint for many spokes, but because it acts like an NBMA cloud, you must use NHRP for address resolution. Third, IPsec profiles bound to the tunnel interface with IKEv2 provide scalable security for dynamic peers; verify SAs with the show crypto commands. Each of these concepts serves a distinct role: mGRE for scalability, NHRP for resolution, and IPsec for security. Keep the three-phase model in mind when planning deployments — Phase 1 for simplicity, Phase 2 for dynamic shortcuts, Phase 3 for full routing optimization. Finally, the verification order IP, NHRP, IPsec, routing helps you quickly isolate common failures. Which one of these will you check first when you next troubleshoot a DMVPN issue?

keyIdea.text: Remember the trio: mGRE for many endpoints, NHRP to resolve addresses, IPsec to secure traffic; verify in that order when troubleshooting.

DMVPN Trio
mGRE, NHRP, IPsec — each has a clear role in scaling and securing the cloud.
NHRP Purpose
Maps tunnel IPs to public IPs so spokes can form direct tunnels on demand.

Confirm IP connectivity, NHRP registrations, IPsec SAs, then routing adjacencies.

screens.title: Key Commands & Troubleshooting Tips
screens.narratorSegment: Keep a short mental checklist when configuring or debugging DMVPN. First, confirm ip nhrp network-id is identical across hub and spokes; mismatches prevent registration. Second, remember to apply crypto ipsec profile to the mGRE tunnel and verify both IKEv2 and IPsec SAs with the show crypto commands. Third, tune MTU and TCP MSS on the tunnel interface to mitigate issues from GRE and IPsec overhead. Verification commands in priority order are: ping the hub public IP, show ip nhrp on hub and spokes, show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa for security status, and show ip eigrp neighbors or show ip ospf neighbor to confirm routing. For a quick lab test, initiate a ping from a host behind one spoke to a host behind another to trigger a spoke-to-spoke tunnel and then check show crypto ipsec sa to see the ephemeral SA. These practical checks will save time and guide you to the root cause faster than changing routing blindly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Commands & Tips
NHRP essentials
ip nhrp network-id, ip nhrp nhs, and ip nhrp map commands must be correct for registration and resolution.
IPsec checks
Use show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa; expect ephemeral SAs after spoke-to-spoke pings.
MTU & MSS
Set ip mtu 1400 and ip tcp adjust-mss 1360 on tunnel interfaces to avoid fragmentation with GRE+IPsec.
Final tip

When troubleshooting, follow the logical order: IP reachability, NHRP registration, IPsec SAs, then routing. This finds root causes faster than random changes.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore Dynamic Multipoint VPN, a design pattern that removes the N-squared tunnel problem by combining multipoint GRE, NHRP, and IPsec. You will learn why DMVPN is used in large enterprise deployments, how the hub and spokes cooperate, and which parts handle address resolution, routing, and security. We will use a concrete three-router scenario — a hub and two spokes — to make the concepts tangible. First, you will understand how mGRE provides a single logical tunnel interface that can terminate many spokes, avoiding dozens or hundreds of unique point-to-point tunnels. Next, you will see how NHRP maps tunnel addresses to public IPs so spokes can build direct shortcuts. Then we'll cover how an IPsec profile secures the GRE traffic using IKEv2 and ESP. Finally, we'll preview Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 trade-offs so you can choose the right model for performance and scalability. As you go through the lesson screens, watch how configuration fragments map to each concept and how simple verification commands reveal the system state. By the end you'll know not just the commands, but how to reason about routing, secure tunnels, and common troubleshooting checks. Which part of the DMVPN stack do you think usually causes the most troubleshooting time in a new deployment?

By the end of this chapter you will describe the architecture and key components of DMVPN, identify how mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec interact, and differentiate the three DMVPN phases and their trade-offs. You will be able to configure a Phase 2 hub-and-spoke DMVPN using IKEv2 and an IPsec profile on Cisco IOS-XE, then integrate a dynamic routing protocol like EIGRP or OSPF to carry internal routes across the DMVPN cloud. Finally, you will learn a troubleshooting workflow: verify public reachability, check NHRP registrations, inspect IPsec SAs, and validate routing adjacencies. Each objective focuses on practical competence: you will read configuration fragments, run verification commands, and interpret outputs to make repair decisions quickly. These skills matter because real-world DMVPNs support many branches and must scale securely; misconfigurations in NHRP, IPsec, or routing type can cause traffic black-holing or slow spoke-to-spoke startup. Expect hands-on practice with the three-router scenario to anchor these objectives in a concrete network.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on configuration and verification steps you will practice. You will build a Phase 2 DMVPN with a hub and two spokes, apply an IKEv2/IPsec profile to the mGRE tunnel, and enable EIGRP over the tunnel to carry internal networks. The lab scenario gives explicit IPs for each router so you can practice commands and verification: hub with 198.51.100.1 and tunnel 172.16.0.1, spokes with 203.0.113.2 and 203.0.113.3 and tunnel addresses 172.16.0.2 and.3. Your verification checklist will use show ip nhrp to confirm registrations, show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa to confirm security associations, and show ip eigrp neighbors to confirm routing adjacencies. You will also practice a spoke-to-spoke ping to trigger dynamic tunnel creation and observe the ephemeral IPsec SA. These verification skills are critical; many real outages are resolved by confirming NHRP registrations or IPsec SA state before changing routing. Practice methodically and note the common misconfigurations described in the lab checklist.

DMVPN solves a fundamental scalability problem in traditional site-to-site VPN designs: the N-squared tunnel explosion. In a full-mesh design each site needs a separate point-to-point tunnel to every other site, which becomes unmanageable as the number of branches grows. DMVPN replaces that static mesh with a single logical multipoint cloud and the ability for spokes to form direct shortcuts when needed. Concretely, this means you configure one mGRE interface on the hub and matching mGRE interfaces on spokes instead of creating many tunnel interfaces. When a spoke wants to reach another spoke it asks the hub for the other spoke's public IP using NHRP and then builds a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel. That dynamic behavior reduces configuration errors and conserves hub bandwidth when spokes talk directly to each other. A common misconception is that DMVPN removes the need for a hub — it does not; the hub is still the registration authority and often the path for multicast or initial control plane traffic. What DMVPN removes is the need for pre-provisioned point-to-point tunnels between every pair of spokes. Think of DMVPN as a taxi-hail system where the hub knows every vehicle's location and directs riders to a direct ride when possible rather than routing each trip through a single central depot. How might this change your network operations when you add dozens of branches?

Multipoint GRE is the foundation that allows DMVPN to scale. Unlike point-to-point GRE, which binds one tunnel interface to a single remote IP, mGRE lets a single tunnel interface accept traffic from many peers without preconfigured destinations. On the hub you configure tunnel mode gre multipoint and a tunnel IP. Spokes configure mGRE as well but initially have their tunnel destination set to the hub's public address for registration. Because the mGRE interface behaves like a non-broadcast multi-access network, devices cannot discover neighbors by simple broadcast and require a discovery mechanism for mapping logical addresses to physical endpoints. This is where NHRP enters. A practical implication is that the hub's tunnel interface must be designed to handle all incoming GRE encapsulated packets and the IPsec profile attached to that interface must be able to secure traffic from any spoke endpoint. A pitfall operators often see is forgetting to set ip mtu and ip tcp adjust-mss to accommodate GRE plus IPsec overhead; this can cause fragmentation or application-level issues. Example: in the lab the hub uses Tunnel0 with 172.16.0.1 and ip mtu 1400 so GRE-over-IPsec packets avoid fragmentation. Remember: mGRE simplifies configuration, but you must plan MTU and security for the multi-tenant tunnel endpoint.

NHRP is the discovery and mapping service that DMVPN uses to match logical tunnel IPs to public physical IPs. The hub acts as the NHRP server, or Next-Hop Server, and every spoke is a client that registers its tunnel IP and public address. When Spoke A wants to send traffic to Spoke B it first consults the hub by querying NHRP for the target's public IP. The hub replies with the mapping and then Spoke A builds a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel to Spoke B. This process is the dynamic shortcut mechanism that keeps traffic off the hub when possible. A concrete example from our lab: R2 registers 172.16.0.2 with the hub; when R2 needs 172.16.0.3 it asks the hub which returns 203.0.113.3, enabling a direct tunnel. A common misinterpretation is to assume NHRP itself carries routing information; it does not. NHRP only resolves addresses. Routing is handled by your dynamic routing protocol over the tunnels. Another operational note: ensure ip nhrp network-id values match across devices; mismatched network-ids prevent registrations. Finish by asking yourself how you would verify NHRP mappings quickly if a spoke reports it cannot reach another spoke.

IPsec provides confidentiality and integrity for GRE-encapsulated DMVPN traffic. The modern best practice is to bind an IPsec profile to the mGRE tunnel interface instead of applying transform sets per peer. An IPsec profile references an IKEv2 profile for key exchange and a transform set for the data plane. Using an IPsec profile simplifies management because the profile applies to any peer that establishes a GRE session over the tunnel, avoiding per-peer crypto map complexity. In our lab we assume a COHORTIA_IPSEC_PROFILE and COHORTIA_IKEV2_PROFILE are already defined; the tunnel interface simply references the profile with the crypto ipsec profile command. A common pitfall is forgetting NAT traversal: if a spoke or hub is behind NAT, you must allow UDP 4500 and 500 and ensure the IKEv2 profile negotiates NAT-T. Another operational note is to inspect IPsec SAs with show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa to confirm both control and data-plane associations. Example: after a spoke-to-spoke shortcut forms, you will see an ephemeral IPsec SA on each spoke corresponding to the direct GRE peer. Verify both sides to confirm symmetric SAs. Remember that security configuration and address resolution are separate responsibilities: NHRP resolves addresses, IPsec secures the resulting GRE tunnels.

DMVPN is commonly discussed in three phases because each phase defines how routing and spoke-to-spoke traffic are handled. Phase 1 is the simplest: hub-and-spoke only. Spoke-to-spoke traffic always traverses the hub, and spokes do not form direct tunnels. This is simple but creates a hub bottleneck. Phase 2 allows spokes to form direct tunnels dynamically using NHRP resolution, but routing may still be hub-centric because the routing protocol advertises spoke networks via the hub. That means the first packet may traverse the hub before the shortcut is built, and care is needed to ensure routing convergence supports shortcuts. Phase 3 moves routing decisions closer to the spokes by allowing NHRP Redirect and Shortcut messages; spokes can learn routes directly and avoid sending initial packets through the hub for route discovery. Phase 3 is the most scalable for many branches, but it requires careful route summarization or modifications at the hub to avoid routing loops. A common misconception is to assume Phase 2 and Phase 3 only change tunnel behavior; they also affect how the routing protocol sees networks. Choose the phase based on whether you prioritize simplicity (Phase 1), quicker path optimization (Phase 2), or fully optimal spoke-to-spoke routing at scale (Phase 3). Which trade-off matters most for your deployment: simplicity or optimal routing?

Phase 1 DMVPN is appropriate when simplicity and strict central control are primary goals. In Phase 1 spokes register with the hub but do not form direct tunnels to other spokes; all traffic is forwarded through the hub. This makes multicast and routing straightforward because the hub remains the single forwarding and registration point. The advantage is ease of configuration and predictable traffic paths. The disadvantage is that spokes communicating with each other use twice the internet bandwidth for the same payload and the hub becomes a potential bottleneck. A concrete example: if Spoke R2 wants to reach Spoke R3 in Phase 1, the packet goes from R2 to the hub's public IP, gets decapsulated and re-encapsulated by the hub, then sent to R3, consuming hub C P U and bandwidth. Operators sometimes mistakenly assume Phase 1 requires less IPsec configuration; in reality, the hub still needs sufficient crypto capacity because it handles all data-plane encryption for spoke traffic. Use Phase 1 in smaller deployments or where policy dictates central inspection or logging of all traffic. Phase 1 details — hub-centric behavior means phase 1 is simplest but forces all spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub, which can cause hub-side bottlenecks.. In practical terms, when all traffic must traverse the hub. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Phase 2 allows spokes to create direct tunnels to one another after an initial resolution via NHRP. The hub still advertises route information in a hub-centric manner, but once a spoke learns another spoke's public IP it can establish a direct GRE-over-IPsec tunnel and exchange traffic directly. This reduces the data path length, improving latency and conserving hub bandwidth. In practical terms: a spoke pings a destination, queries the hub, receives the remote public IP, builds a direct tunnel, and then subsequent traffic uses the shortcut. However, routing can still be a source of confusion because routing advertisements may cause traffic to be forwarded via the hub until the shortcut is established. Misconfigurations often relate to OSPF network types or forgetting ip nhrp map multicast dynamic on the hub so multicast routing updates do not flow correctly to spokes. For a lab example, using EIGRP over the tunnel generally works without changing network types, whereas OSPF may require ip ospf network broadcast or non-broadcast settings on the hub to ensure neighbors form correctly over the NBMA cloud. In summary, Phase 2 is a useful middle ground: better than Phase 1 for traffic efficiency, but still requires careful routing behavior checks.

Phase 3 introduces NHRP Redirect and Shortcut messages to make routing optimal for spoke-to-spoke communications. Rather than just forming a temporary direct tunnel after address resolution, the hub can send a redirect telling a spoke that a better path exists and provide information so the spokes update routing directly. This lets spokes learn routes from each other in a way that avoids repeated hub involvement for routing decisions. Practically this reduces hub load and avoids hairpinning after the first packet. Implementing Phase 3 requires careful consideration at the hub: you may need to summarize or manipulate advertised routes so the hub's routing entries allow proper redirect behavior without creating loops. A misconception is to assume Phase 3 is a drop-in replacement for Phase 2; routing behavior changes and must be validated in lab conditions. Use Phase 3 when you have many spokes and want the most efficient runtime forwarding, and ensure your routing strategy supports NHRP redirect messaging. As you plan, ask how route advertisement at the hub will affect redirects and whether summarization is necessary to avoid overlapping advertisements.

The hub must use ip nhrp map multicast dynamic so multicast routing updates reach spokes and the spokes can learn multicast-required protocols. Let's consolidate the most important facts. First, DMVPN combines mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec to let spokes create on-demand tunnels that scale far better than static full-mesh VPNs. Second, mGRE provides a single logical tunnel endpoint for many spokes, but because it acts like an NBMA cloud, you must use NHRP for address resolution. Third, IPsec profiles bound to the tunnel interface with IKEv2 provide scalable security for dynamic peers; verify SAs with the show crypto commands. Each of these concepts serves a distinct role: mGRE for scalability, NHRP for resolution, and IPsec for security. Keep the three-phase model in mind when planning deployments — Phase 1 for simplicity, Phase 2 for dynamic shortcuts, Phase 3 for full routing optimization. Finally, the verification order IP, NHRP, IPsec, routing helps you quickly isolate common failures. Which one of these will you check first when you next troubleshoot a DMVPN issue?

Keep a short mental checklist when configuring or debugging DMVPN. First, confirm ip nhrp network-id is identical across hub and spokes; mismatches prevent registration. Second, remember to apply crypto ipsec profile to the mGRE tunnel and verify both IKEv2 and IPsec SAs with the show crypto commands. Third, tune MTU and TCP MSS on the tunnel interface to mitigate issues from GRE and IPsec overhead. Verification commands in priority order are: ping the hub public IP, show ip nhrp on hub and spokes, show crypto ikev2 sa and show crypto ipsec sa for security status, and show ip eigrp neighbors or show ip ospf neighbor to confirm routing. For a quick lab test, initiate a ping from a host behind one spoke to a host behind another to trigger a spoke-to-spoke tunnel and then check show crypto ipsec sa to see the ephemeral SA. These practical checks will save time and guide you to the root cause faster than changing routing blindly.
